section.concept: Composition of Functions: The composition of functions $$f$$ and $$g,$$ is written $$f \circ g$$ and is defined by $$\left( {f \circ g} \right)(x) = f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ We read $$f\left( {g(x)} \right)$$ as $$f$$ of $$g$$ of $$x.$$
Horizontal Line Test: If every horizontal line, intersects the graph of a function in at most one point, it is a one-to-one function.

Inverse of a Function Defined by Ordered Pairs: If $$f(x)$$ is a one-to-one function whose ordered pairs are of the form $$\left( {x,y} \right),$$ then its inverse function $$f^{-1}(x)$$ is the set of ordered pairs $$\left( {y,x} \right).$$

Inverse Functions: For every $$x$$ in the domain of one-to-one function $$f$$ and $$f^{-1},$$ $$\begin{array}{rll} {f^{-1}\left( {f(x)} \right)} & = & x \\ {f\left( {f^{-1}(x)} \right)} & = & x \end{array}$$

How to Find the Inverse of a One-to-One Function:
Step 1. Substitute y for $$f(x).$$ Step 2. Interchange the variables x and y. Step 3. Solve for y. Step 4. Substitute $$f^{-1}(x)$$ for $$y.$$ Step 5. Verify that the functions are inverses.

One-to-One Property of Exponential Functions: For $$a > 0$$ and $$a \neq 1,$$ $$\text{If}\ a^{x} = a^{y},\ \text{then}\ x = y.$$

How to Solve an Exponential Equation
Step 1. Write both sides of the equation with the same base, if possible. Step 2. Write a new equation by setting the exponents equal. Step 3. Solve the equation. Step 4. Check the solution.

Compound Interest: For a principal, $$P,$$ invested at an interest rate, $$r,$$ for $$t$$ years, the new balance, $$A,$$ is $$\begin{array}{lccccl} & & & & & \\ & & & & & \\ {A = P\left( {1 + \frac{r}{n}} \right)^{nt}} & & & & & {\text{when compounded}\ n\ \text{times a year.}} \\ {A = Pe^{rt}} & & & & & \text{when compounded continuously.} \end{array}$$
Exponential Growth and Decay: For an original amount, $$A_{0}$$ that grows or decays at a rate, $$r,$$ for a certain time $$t,$$ the final amount,$$A,$$ is $$A = A_{0}e^{rt}.$$

Decibel Level of Sound: The loudness level, $$D$$, measured in decibels, of a sound of intensity, $$I$$, measured in watts per square inch is $$D = 10\text{log}\left( \frac{I}{10^{-12}} \right).$$
Earthquake Intensity: The magnitude $$R$$ of an earthquake is measured by $$R = \text{log}\ I,$$ where $$I$$ is the intensity of its shock wave.
Properties of Logarithms $$\mspace{54mu}\text{log}_{a}1 = 0\mspace{90mu}\text{log}_{a}a = 1$$

Inverse Properties of Logarithms
For $$a > 0,$$$$x > 0$$ and $$a \neq 1$$ $$a^{\text{log}_{a}x} = x\mspace{89mu}\text{log}_{a}a^{x} = x$$

Product Property of Logarithms
If $$M > 0,N > 0\text{,}\ \text{a} > 0$$ and $$\text{a} \neq 1,$$ then, $$\mspace{37mu}\text{log}_{a}M \cdot N = \text{log}_{a}M + \text{log}_{a}N$$ The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms.

Quotient Property of Logarithms
If $$M > 0,N > 0\text{,}\ \text{a} > 0$$ and $$\text{a} \neq 1,$$ then, $$\mspace{54mu}\text{log}_{a}\frac{M}{N} = \text{log}_{a}M - \text{log}_{a}N$$ The logarithm of a quotient is the difference of the logarithms.

Power Property of Logarithms
If $$M > 0,\ \text{a} > 0,\ \text{a} \neq 1$$ and $$p$$ is any real number then, $$\text{log}_{a}M^{p} = p\ \text{log}_{a}M$$ The log of a number raised to a power is the product of the power times the log of the number.

Change-of-Base Formula For any logarithmic bases a and b, and $$M > 0,$$ $$\begin{matrix} {\text{log}_{a}M = \frac{\text{log}_{b}M}{\text{log}_{b}a}} & & & {\qquad\text{log}_{a}M = \frac{\text{log}M}{\text{log}a}} & & & {\qquad\text{log}_{a}M = \frac{\text{ln}\ M}{\text{ln}\ a}} \\ {\text{new base}\ b} & & & {\qquad\text{new base 10}} & & & {\qquad\text{new base}\ e} \end{matrix}$$
One-to-One Property of Logarithmic Equations: For $$M > 0,N > 0,\ a\ \text{>}\ 0,$$ and $$\text{a} \neq 1$$ is any real number: $$\text{If}\ \text{log}_{a}M = \text{log}_{a}N,\ \text{then}\ M = N.$$

Exponential Growth and Decay: For an original amount, $$A_{0}$$ that grows or decays at a rate, r, for a certain time t, the final amount, A, is $$A = A_{0}e^{rt}.$$
